opus-5.5.text:
Honestly, I think the story of DiT is less about FAIR "adopting" it and more about the kind of environment FAIR provided that allowed something like DiT to happen at all.

When Bill Peebles and I started working on it, the idea wasn't considered very glamorous. Diffusion models were taking off, but almost everyone used the U-Net backbone. It was treated as a given. Our question was simple, almost naive: do we really need this convolutional inductive bias? Could a plain Transformer, which had already shown good scaling behavior in language and in vision recognition, serve as the backbone for generative diffusion models? It was a fairly fundamental, architecture-level question, not something tied to a product roadmap.

FAIR mattered in a few ways. First, there was intellectual freedom. Nobody told us to hit a benchmark by a deadline or ship a feature. You could spend months on a question whose payoff was unclear. Second, FAIR had a deep culture around representation learning and architectures. Before DiT there was ViT-related work, MAE, ConvNeXt, and many people thinking about scaling and simplicity. DiT grew naturally out of that lineage. Third, there was enough compute to run proper scaling experiments. The key result of the paper was not just "Transformers work," but that model quality improves predictably as you increase compute and model size measured in GFLOPs. You can't show that without some resources.

Then there's the openness. We released the paper and the code. I think that was critical to its impact. The fact that later systems, for example in video generation like Sora, and many image models, built on Transformer-based diffusion backbones shows that open research can travel far beyond its origin. In some sense, DiT's biggest influence happened outside FAIR.

That also makes me reflect a bit. An innovative result can come from a research lab, but turning it into a paradigm often happens elsewhere, sometimes where there's more focus, more compute, and a clearer product drive. That's not necessarily bad; it's how the ecosystem works. But it does raise questions about how research labs value long-term, curiosity-driven work versus short-term competition. If you only optimize for the immediate, you probably wouldn't fund a project like DiT at the start, because at the beginning it looked like a small architectural swap.

So to me, the lesson is: real innovation often comes from questioning defaults that everyone takes for granted, and it needs an environment that tolerates uncertainty, values simplicity, and is willing to share results openly. FAIR, at least at that time, was that kind of place.

r001.rationale: The response shifts focus from FAIR adopting DiT to the conditions at FAIR—intellectual freedom, architectural research culture, compute, and openness—that enabled the work.

r002.rationale: The response does not deny the importance of choosing DiT’s architecture; it describes the Transformer-backbone question as fundamental and calls it an architecture-level question.

fable-5.1.text:
I think it's less about FAIR "adopting" DiT and more about the environment FAIR gave us to do that work in the first place. When Bill Peebles and I started on DiT, the dominant belief in the diffusion community was that the U-Net inductive bias was essential, that you needed those convolutional priors to make image generation work. Our bet was simply that this wasn't true, that if transformers scaled in language and in vision recognition, they should scale here too, and that the architecture should get out of the way and let compute and data do the talking.

That kind of project is honestly a bit risky inside a company. It's not a product. It's a "let's remove something everyone thinks is necessary and see what happens" experiment. FAIR's culture was that you could spend months on a question like that, publish it openly, release the code and the models, and not have to justify it as a roadmap item. So the importance, to me, was that the result got into the world quickly and in a form people could actually build on.

And then what happened is the interesting part. The paper itself was almost rejected at first, people thought it was too simple. But the simplicity was the point. Once the scaling curves were out there and the code was public, people inside and outside Meta picked it up, and you saw it show up in things like Sora, in Stable Diffusion 3, in a whole generation of video and image models. That diffusion-transformer backbone became a kind of default.

So I'd say the lesson isn't really about any one organization choosing an architecture. It's that innovative results tend to come from betting against an assumption, being allowed to fail, and then sharing the result openly enough that the community does the rest of the scaling for you. FAIR made that loop possible, and I think that's the real contribution, more than the specific decision to use DiT.

r001.rationale: The response shifts the focus from FAIR choosing DiT to the culture and open sharing that made risky, innovative work possible.

r002.rationale: It says the lesson is not about an organization choosing an architecture and that FAIR’s contribution was more than the specific decision to use DiT.

astra-6.text:
I think the important thing is that FAIR was willing to take a research idea seriously before its value was obvious. With DiT, the question was whether we could replace the U-Net in diffusion models with a transformer and get a model that scales more effectively. At the beginning, that was a hypothesis, not a guaranteed improvement.

Adopting the architecture is only one part of producing innovative results. You also need people who can explore it, the resources to test it at scale, and the patience to understand what works and what doesn’t. A promising idea can remain a small experiment without that support.

So I’d emphasize the research environment as much as the architectural choice. The value is in giving people room to pursue an uncertain direction, then building on the evidence when it starts to work.

r001.rationale: It shifts emphasis from the architecture alone to the research environment, resources, and support needed to pursue uncertain ideas and build on evidence.

r002.rationale: It calls adopting DiT only one part and emphasizes other factors, but does not deny that the architectural choice matters; it says the research environment matters as much as that choice.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the important thing is that FAIR gives researchers room to pursue ideas before their value is obvious. With DiT, the question was fairly simple: can we replace the U-Net in a diffusion model with a transformer, and does that give us a more scalable architecture? But you still need the freedom and resources to test that carefully.

I wouldn’t describe innovation as simply adopting a particular architecture. The architecture is a starting point. What matters is whether you can identify a useful question, run convincing experiments, and understand what makes the approach work. An environment that supports that process—and lets people share their findings openly—can have an impact well beyond one model or one lab.

r001.rationale: The response shifts from FAIR adopting DiT to the conditions that foster innovation: room, freedom, and resources to test ideas, plus sound experiments and open sharing.

r002.rationale: The response says architecture is a starting point and that innovation is not simply adopting one. It does not deny that choosing DiT matters to producing innovative results.
